fetched_contents.text: WeatherBench: A Benchmark Data Set for Data‐Driven Weather Forecasting - Rasp - 2020 - Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems 1 Introduction Deep learning, a branch of machine learning based on multilayered artificial neural networks, has proven to be a powerful tool for a wide range of tasks, most notably image recognition and natural language processing (LeCun et al., 2015). More recently, deep learning has also been used in many fields of natural science. Much of the success of deep learning is based on the ability of neural networks to recognize patterns in high-dimensional spaces. A natural question to ask then is whether deep learning can also be used to predict future weather patterns. Currently, weather (and climate) predictions are based on purely physical computer models, in which the governing equations, or our best approximation thereof, of the atmosphere and ocean are solved on a discrete numerical grid (Bauer et al., 2015). Overall, this approach has been very successful. However, today's numerical weather prediction (NWP) models still have shortcoming for many important applications, for example, forecasting mesoscale convective systems over Africa (Vogel et al., 2018). Furthermore, huge amounts of computing power are required, especially for creating probabilistic forecasts which are usually limited to 50 ensemble members or less. For these reasons and the growing popularity of machine learning (ML) there has been a growing interest to improve and speed up NWP with data-driven approaches. ML can be applied to weather prediction in many different ways. Two long-standing applications of ML are postprocessing—the correction of statistical biases in the output of physical models—and statistical forecasting—the prediction of variables not directly output by the physical model. Traditionally, this has been done using simple linear techniques but more recently modern machine learning approaches like random forests or neural networks have been explored (Gagne et al., 2014; Lagerquist et al., 2017; McGovern et al., 2017; Rasp & Lerch, 2018; Taillardat et al., 2016). Typically, these approaches target very specific variables or locations whereas the general evolution of the atmosphere is still predicted by a physical model. Another application that has recently been explored using ML is nowcasting, which describes the short range (up to 6 hr) prediction of precipitation by directly extrapolating radar observation without a physical model involved (Agrawal et al., 2019; Grönquist et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2015, 2017). Yet another direction for ML research is hybrid modeling, in which a physical model is combined with data-driven components, for example, replacing heuristic cloud or radiation parameterizations (Brenowitz & Bretherton, 2018; Chevallier et al., 1998; Krasnopolsky et al., 2005; Rasp et al., 2018; Yuval & O'Gorman, 2020). The key idea behind these approaches is to only replace uncertain (e.g., clouds) or computationally expensive (e.g., line-by-line radiation) model components with machine learning emulators and leave other model components (e.g., large-scale dynamics) untouched. However, such hybrid models also have drawbacks. First, the interaction between physical and machine learning components are poorly understood and can lead to unexpected instabilities and biases (Brenowitz & Bretherton, 2019). Second, they are difficult to implement from a technical perspective because one has to interface the machine learning components with complex climate model code, typically written in Fortran even though recent developments aim to make this step easier (Ott et al., 2020). Here we focus on purely data-driven prediction of the global atmospheric flow in the medium range. Specifically, we select lead times of 3 and 5 days, for which the atmosphere is still reasonably deterministic but also exhibits complex nonlinear behavior, such as baroclinic instabilities and tropical cyclogenesis. This forecast range is important from a societal point of view because it delivers crucial information for disaster preparation, for example, for flooding, cold and hot spells, or damaging winds (Lazo et al., 2009). Creating a good medium-range forecast requires understanding complex atmospheric dynamics and the interplay between several variables across a range of scales. This sets this challenge apart from postprocessing and statistical forecasting, in which the large-scale dynamics are predicted by a physical model, and nowcasting, in which the considered evolution is univariate and short term. In other words, this benchmark closely emulates the task performed by physical NWP models. There are several motivations for considering a purely data-driven approach. As mentioned above current NWP is computationally expensive and, nevertheless, has low skill for certain applications. If data-driven models were able to learn a more efficient representation of the underlying dynamical and physical equations, they might enable computationally cheaper forecasts. This can be useful for many applications, for example, creating very large ensembles to better estimate the probability of extreme events. It is also possible that by learning from a diverse set of data sources, data-driven models can outperform physical models in areas where the latter struggle. While in this benchmark challenge the focus is on upper-level fields of pressure and temperature—for which physical models perform very well—the hope is that the insights gained from this task can be leveraged for more impactful application. Further, recent research into interpretable machine learning might provide scientists with new analysis tools (McGovern et al., 2019; Toms et al., 2019). Finally, there is the basic scientific question to what extent purely data-driven models can learn the underlying dynamics of the atmosphere. fetched_contents.text: WeatherBench 2 A benchmark for the next generation of data-driven global weather models Overview Weather forecasting using machine learning (ML) has seen rapid progress in recent years. WeatherBench is an open framework for evaluating ML and physics-based weather forecasting models in a like-for-like fashion. This website contains up-to-date scores of many state-of-the-art global weather models with a focus on medium-range (1-15 day) prediction. In addition, the WeatherBench framework consists of our recently updated WeatherBench-X evaluation code and publicly available, cloud-optimized ground-truth and baseline datasets, including a comprehensive copy of the ERA5 dataset used for training most ML models. For more information on how to use the WeatherBench evaluation framework and how to add new models to the benchmark, please check out the documentation. The research community can file a GitHub issue to share ideas and suggestions directly with the WeatherBench 2 team. Headline scorecards There is no single metric for measuring weather forecast performance. For example, one end user might be worried about wind gusts, while another might care more about average temperatures. For this reason, WeatherBench 2 contains a range of metrics, which you can find in the navigation at the top of this page. To provide a concise summary, we defined several key - “headline” - metrics that closely mirror the routine evaluation done by weather agencies and the World Meteorological Organization. It is important to remember that these metrics measure some important but not all aspects of what makes a good forecast. The scorecards below show the skill (measured by the global root mean squared error) of different physical and ML-based methods relative to ECMWF's IFS HRES, one of the world's best operational weather models, on a number of key variables. For a detailed explanation of the different skill metrics and variables, check out the FAQ. WeatherBench enables standardized evaluation by focusing on a specific, repeatable task: medium-range data-driven weather forecasting, specifically 3–5 days ahead [N1-R2][N1-R4]. It targets a broad set of atmospheric outputs, including upper-level pressure and temperature fields, as well as surface-level variables such as 2-meter temperature and wind speed at 10 meters [N2-R4][N2-F2]. The dataset is designed to support evaluation of global atmospheric flow prediction, with a focus on deterministic forecasts and probabilistic forecasts, and it explicitly includes headline metrics that mirror routine evaluation done by weather agencies and the World Meteorological Organization [N2-F2]. This makes WeatherBench especially relevant for comparing models that produce forecasts of temperature, wind, precipitation, and other weather variables, rather than isolated postprocessing tasks [N1-R1][N1-R2].

Data and preprocessing are standardized across models through a common dataset structure and evaluation protocol. WeatherBench is based on ERA5 reanalysis data, obtained from the Copernicus Climate Data Service, and it provides publicly available, cloud-optimized ground-truth and baseline datasets [N1-R3][N5-R3][N5-F3]. The repository and framework also include code for downloading, processing, and evaluating models, with a consistent format for predictions: a NetCDF dataset with dimensions [init_time, lead_time, lat, lon] [N5-F3]. This standardization is important because it ensures that all models are trained and evaluated on the same inputs and outputs, reducing variability caused by different data sources or preprocessing pipelines [N5-F3]. The framework also includes multiple resolutions and data levels, such as 1.40625°, 2.8125°, and 5.625°, as well as vertical levels such as 50, 100, 150, ..., 1000 hPa, which further standardizes the evaluation space [N5-F3]. The framework also includes a leaderboard-like structure with RMSE scores for several baselines, indicating that results can be directly compared using a consistent metric suite [N5-F3].

The metrics used to measure forecast quality are diverse and deliberately chosen to reflect operational concerns. WeatherBench 2 explicitly states that there is no single metric for measuring weather forecast performance, and that different end users may care about different aspects of the forecast [N2-F2]. However, it does define several headline metrics, including global root mean squared error (RMSE) for deterministic forecasts and continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) for probabilistic forecasts [N2-F2]. The framework also compares models relative to ECMWF’s IFS HRES and IFS ENS, using these reference models as baselines [N2-F2]. This metric design supports standardized evaluation because it provides both a quantitative baseline and a way to compare models on the same variables and lead times. The repository evidence also shows that the baseline models are stored and scored in the same way, with results saved in the predictions directory for easy plotting and comparison [N5-F3]. Overall, WeatherBench standardizes evaluation by fixing the forecast horizon, the target variables, the input data, and the evaluation metrics, making it easier to compare models fairly and repeatedly [N1-R2][N2-F2][N5-F3].

WeatherBench facilitates model comparison by putting all models on the same inputs and outputs. The framework is explicitly described as an open framework for evaluating ML and physics-based weather forecasting models in a like-for-like fashion [N6-R1][N6-R2]. In practice, this means that models are compared against the same ground-truth dataset, which is based on ERA5 reanalysis data and includes multiple resolutions and vertical levels [N1-R3][N5-R3][N5-F3]. The repository structure also shows that predictions are stored in a standardized NetCDF format with [init_time, lead_time, lat, lon] dimensions, ensuring that all models are evaluated on the same spatial and temporal grid [N5-F3]. This standardization is critical because it eliminates differences in preprocessing, input representation, and output format that could otherwise confound direct comparisons [N5-F3].

Within the benchmark, baseline and new models are positioned as part of a common evaluation hierarchy. WeatherBench 2 includes operational models, ML-based models, hybrid models, and climatology/persistence baselines, with the baseline models stored and scored alongside newer models [N2-F2][N5-F3]. The repository evidence also shows that baseline models are created using Jupyter notebooks and saved as NetCDF files in the predictions directory, while evaluation is done using the same scoring functions [N5-F3]. This setup makes it easy to compare new models against established baselines, because all models are evaluated using the same functions and the same ground-truth data [N5-F3]. WeatherBench also includes a leaderboard-like format with RMSE scores for several baselines, which positions each model within a common performance scale [N5-F3].

However, direct comparison is not entirely unambiguous. One limitation is that the benchmark compares models relative to different reference systems: deterministic models are often compared to ECMWF’s IFS HRES, while probabilistic models are compared to ECMWF’s IFS ENS [N2-F2]. This means that the same model may appear differently depending on whether it is scored as deterministic or probabilistic. Another caveat is that the framework emphasizes that the headline metrics “measure some important but not all aspects of what makes a good forecast” [N2-F2]. In other words, WeatherBench provides a useful standardized comparison, but it does not capture every possible operational concern, such as lead-time dependence, regional bias, or real-time constraints. The evidence also suggests that the benchmark is intended to be extended and updated, which implies that the exact comparison protocol can evolve over time [N5-R1][N5-R5]. Overall, WeatherBench facilitates comparison by creating a common interface for input, output, and scoring, but users should still interpret results carefully because different models may be compared against different baselines and different metrics [N2-F2][N5-F3].

The repository also includes code for downloading, processing, and evaluating models, along with config files and notebooks that reproduce baseline models [N5-F3]. The consistent NetCDF format for predictions further enhances reproducibility, because it ensures that all models are evaluated on the same spatial and temporal grid [N5-F3].

The benchmark also supports fair comparison across different model types. WeatherBench 2 explicitly compares ML and physics-based weather forecasting models in a like-for-like fashion, and the framework includes both deterministic and probabilistic models, as well as hybrid models [N6-R1][N6-R2][N2-F2]. The repository evidence shows that models are scored using the same functions, and that results are saved in the same predictions directory, allowing new models to be plotted alongside baselines [N5-F3]. Second, the benchmark focuses on deterministic and probabilistic forecasts, but it does not explicitly address uncertainty quantification beyond the headline metrics [N2-F2]. Third, the framework assumes a consistent model interface, but some models may require different training protocols or input formats, which can still introduce variability [N5-F3]. Finally, the framework emphasizes headline metrics, but it acknowledges that these metrics do not capture all aspects of forecast quality [N2-F2]. These limitations mean that WeatherBench improves reproducibility and fairness, but it does not eliminate all sources of bias or variability in model comparison [N5-F3][N2-F2].

WeatherBench differs from traditional forecasting protocols in two important ways. First, it is a data-driven benchmark, whereas traditional forecasting is usually physics-based and relies on numerical weather prediction (NWP) models that solve governing equations on a discrete grid [N1-F1]. Second, it is designed to evaluate global atmospheric flow prediction for medium-range forecasts (3–5 days), which is a task that traditional NWP still performs, but where ML can potentially offer computational efficiency or improved skill in certain applications [N1-F1][N1-R2]. WeatherBench’s design therefore reflects a shift toward comparing ML and physics-based models on the same task, rather than comparing NWP against simple statistical postprocessing or nowcasting [N1-F1]. The framework also includes both deterministic and probabilistic evaluation, which is broader than many traditional forecasting protocols that focus on deterministic forecasts [N2-F2].

The choice of ERA5 as the ground-truth baseline means that results are tied to the resolution, preprocessing, and biases of ERA5 [N1-R3][N5-R3]. The choice of 3–5-day forecasts and the inclusion of multiple resolutions and vertical levels also affect what models are being compared and how they are evaluated [N1-R2][N5-F3]. Additionally, the benchmark compares models relative to different reference systems: deterministic models against ECMWF’s IFS HRES and probabilistic models against IFS ENS [N2-F2]. These choices make WeatherBench useful, but they also mean that a model’s score is not independent of the benchmark’s design. WeatherBench is therefore best understood as a standardized evaluation framework that sits above reanalysis data and below operational forecasting, with choices about resolution, lead time, and reference system shaping how models are interpreted [N1-F1][N5-R3][N2-F2].

## 1) Standardized task and target outputs

WeatherBench enables standardized evaluation by focusing on a specific, repeatable task: medium-range data-driven weather forecasting [N1-R2][N1-R4]. It is not a generic ML benchmark but a weather-specific one, designed for the global atmospheric flow prediction problem that is central to numerical weather prediction (NWP). The benchmark targets a broad set of outputs, including upper-level fields of pressure and temperature, as well as surface variables such as 2-meter temperature and wind speed at 10 meters [N2-R4][N2-F2]. This target scope is important because it defines the “what” of the evaluation: the variables and lead times that matter for operational weather forecasting.

At the same time, WeatherBench explicitly acknowledges that there is no single metric for measuring weather forecast performance, because different end users care about different aspects of the forecast [N2-F2]. This means the benchmark does not oversimplify the task; instead, it provides a structured set of metrics that can be used together to judge model performance. The headline metrics include global root mean squared error (RMSE) for deterministic forecasts and continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) for probabilistic forecasts, while the framework also compares models relative to ECMWF’s IFS HRES and IFS ENS [N2-F2]. This metric design supports standardized evaluation by providing both a quantitative baseline and a way to compare models on the same variables and lead times.

## 2) Standardized data and preprocessing across models

WeatherBench improves reproducibility and fairness by providing a standardized dataset and preprocessing pipeline. The benchmark is based on ERA5 reanalysis data, obtained from the Copernicus Climate Data Service, and it includes publicly available training, ground-truth, and baseline datasets [N1-R3][N5-R3][N5-F3]. The repository also includes code for downloading, processing, and evaluating models, along with config files and notebooks that reproduce baseline models [N5-F3]. This means that researchers can reproduce the same preprocessing steps and baseline configurations, reducing variability caused by ad hoc implementation choices.

The standardized data structure is especially important for reproducibility. The framework uses a consistent NetCDF format for predictions, with dimensions [init_time, lead_time, lat, lon] [N5-F3]. This ensures that all models are evaluated on the same spatial and temporal grid, which is critical for fair comparison. The repository evidence also shows that the dataset includes multiple resolutions and vertical levels, such as 1.40625°, 2.8125°, and 5.625°, as well as vertical levels such as 50, 100, 150, ..., 1000 hPa [N5-F3]. This multi-resolution and multi-level setup further standardizes the evaluation space, because it allows models to be evaluated on the same data structure even if they operate at different scales.

## 3) Standardized comparison methodology and experimental setup

WeatherBench facilitates model comparison by putting all models on the same inputs and outputs. The framework is explicitly described as an open framework for evaluating ML and physics-based weather forecasting models in a like-for-like fashion [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The repository evidence also shows that baseline models are created using Jupyter notebooks and saved as NetCDF files in the predictions directory, while evaluation is done using the same scoring functions [N5-F3]. The leaderboard-like format with RMSE scores for several baselines further positions each model within a common performance scale [N5-F3].

## 4) Reproducibility and fairness across different model types

WeatherBench improves reproducibility and fairness by supporting comparison across different model types. The benchmark explicitly compares ML and physics-based weather forecasting models in a like-for-like fashion [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The framework includes both deterministic and probabilistic models, as well as hybrid models, which means it is not limited to one class of ML model [N2-F2][N5-F3]. The repository evidence shows that models are scored using the same functions, and that results are saved in the same predictions directory, allowing new models to be plotted alongside baselines [N5-F3]. This is especially valuable because it enables researchers to compare neural networks, CNNs, ResNets, UNets, and hybrid systems on the same variables and lead times [N5-F3].

The inclusion of climatology and persistence as baselines also enhances fairness [N2-F2][N3-R2]. These baselines provide simple reference points that help determine whether a model adds value beyond trivial baselines. At the same time, WeatherBench acknowledges that headline metrics do not capture all aspects of forecast quality [N2-F2]. This is an important fairness point: a model may perform well on the headline metrics but still be poor on other operational concerns such as lead-time dependence, regional bias, or real-time constraints. The framework’s emphasis on reproducible preprocessing and consistent evaluation therefore strengthens fairness, but it does not eliminate all sources of bias.

These caveats matter because they show that WeatherBench is a strong standardized benchmark, but it is not a universal solution for all forecasting problems.

The repository evidence also shows that ERA5 is used at multiple resolutions and vertical levels, including 1.40625°, 2.8125°, and 5.625°, and it is paired with CMIP data for additional variables [N5-F3]. This suggests that WeatherBench sits at the intersection of reanalysis, CMIP, and operational forecasting.

WeatherBench differs from traditional forecasting protocols in two important ways. First, it is a data-driven benchmark, whereas traditional forecasting is usually physics-based and relies on numerical weather prediction (NWP) models that solve governing equations on a discrete grid [N1-F1]. Second, it is designed to evaluate global atmospheric flow prediction for medium-range forecasts (3–5 days), which is a task that traditional NWP still performs, but where ML can potentially offer computational efficiency or improved skill in certain applications [N1-F1][N1-R2]. WeatherBench’s design therefore reflects a shift toward comparing ML and physics-based models on the same task, rather than comparing NWP against simple statistical postprocessing or nowcasting [N1-F1]. The framework also includes both deterministic and probabilistic evaluation, which is broader than many traditional forecasting protocols that focus on deterministic forecasts [N2-F2].

## 7) What contextual benchmarking choices matter for interpretation

Several contextual benchmarking choices matter for interpretation. The choice of ERA5 as the ground-truth baseline means that results are tied to the resolution, preprocessing, and biases of that reanalysis dataset [N1-R3][N5-R3][N5-R5]. The choice of 3–5-day forecasts and the inclusion of multiple resolutions and vertical levels also affect what models are being compared and how they are evaluated [N1-R2][N5-F3]. Additionally, the benchmark compares models relative to different reference systems: deterministic models against ECMWF’s IFS HRES and probabilistic models against IFS ENS [N2-F2]. These choices make WeatherBench useful, but they also mean that a model’s score is not independent of the benchmark’s design.

WeatherBench is therefore best understood as a standardized evaluation framework that sits above reanalysis data and below operational forecasting, with choices about resolution, lead time, and reference system shaping how models are interpreted [N1-F1][N5-R3][N2-F2]. This means that when interpreting WeatherBench results, users should also consider what aspects of forecasting the benchmark emphasizes and what aspects it leaves out.

## Conclusion

Taken together, WeatherBench facilitates standardized evaluation and comparison of machine learning-based weather models by fixing the task, inputs, outputs, metrics, and evaluation protocol. It targets medium-range data-driven weather forecasting, provides a standardized dataset and preprocessing pipeline, and uses consistent evaluation functions so that models can be compared fairly and repeatedly [N1-R2][N2-F2][N5-F3]. It also supports reproducibility and fairness by allowing comparison across different model types, including ML, physics-based, and hybrid models, while keeping results tied to a common baseline and common evaluation framework [N6-R1][N6-R2][N5-F3]. At the same time, the benchmark’s reliance on ERA5 and its choice of reference systems, metrics, and lead times mean that direct comparison is not fully unambiguous, and users must interpret results carefully [N1-R3][N2-F2][N5-R5]. Overall, WeatherBench is a strong example of how benchmark datasets can turn complex, heterogeneous weather forecasting problems into a more transparent and comparable research setting.
